p.src: Now Tang Sanzang and his two disciples, having escaped their ordeal, journeyed onward. Before many days had passed, they crossed Yellow Wind Ridge and continued west into a broad expanse of level country. Time flew swiftly; summer passed into autumn, when chill cicadas sang among withered willows and the Fire Star sank westward. As they traveled, they suddenly came upon a vast torrent, its turbid waters surging in billows. From horseback Sanzang called out anxiously, “Disciples, look how broad the waters are ahead! Why are there no boats plying them? Where are we to cross?” Bajie looked and said, “It truly is a raging torrent, with no boat to carry us across.” The Pilgrim leaped into the air and shaded his eyes with one hand to look. Even he was alarmed. “Master,” he said, “this truly is difficult, truly difficult. If it were only old Monkey crossing this river, I would merely twist my waist and be over it; but for Master, it would be a thousandfold difficult to cross and impossible to pass even in ten thousand years.” Sanzang said, “As far as I can see, it has no end. Just how wide is it?” The Pilgrim replied, “It is about eight hundred li across.” Bajie asked, “Brother, how can you be so sure of the distance?” The Pilgrim said, “To tell you the truth, worthy brother, by daylight these eyes of old Monkey can ordinarily discern good and ill fortune a thousand li away. Looking from the air just now, I could not tell how far the river stretches upstream or downstream, but its breadth before us is certainly a full eight hundred li.” The elder lamented in troubled distress and turned his horse back, when he suddenly saw a stone monument standing on the bank. All three went over to inspect it. They saw three characters in seal script at the top: “River of Flowing Sands”; and below them were four short lines in regular script, which read:

p.src: The Great Sage stayed beside Tang Sanzang, holding the horse and guarding the luggage. When he saw Bajie battling the monster, he ground his teeth with impatience and rubbed his palms and clenched his fists. Unable to restrain himself from joining the fight, he drew his cudgel and said, “Master, sit here and do not be afraid. Let old Monkey go and have a little sport with him.” His master pleaded bitterly with him, but could not keep him back. With a shrill whistle, he leaped to the front. The monster and Bajie were then at the fiercest point of their contest, locked in an inextricable struggle. The Pilgrim swung up his iron cudgel and brought it down upon the monster’s head. The monster spun around, narrowly dodged the blow, and plunged straight into the River of Flowing Sands. Bajie was so angry that he jumped about wildly. “Brother!” he cried. “Who asked you to come? The monster’s hands were slowing, and he could hardly parry my rake. In another three or five rounds I would have captured him. He saw how fierce you were and fled the field. What are we to do now?” The Pilgrim laughed. “Brother, to tell you the truth, since we subdued the Yellow Wind Monster and came down from the mountain, I have not had a chance to wield my cudgel for over a month. When I saw what a fine fight you two were having, my feet began itching and I could not resist jumping in for a little sport. How was I to know that the monster could not take a joke and would run away?”

p.src: Arm in arm, the two talked and laughed as they returned to Tang Sanzang. Tang Sanzang asked, “Did you capture the monster?” The Pilgrim replied, “The monster could not withstand us. He was defeated and fled back beneath the water.” Sanzang said, “Disciple, that monster has lived here a long time and knows the depth and shallows. With such a boundless stretch of treacherous water and no boats or oars, we must have someone who knows its ways to guide us across.” The Pilgrim said, “That is exactly right. As the saying goes, ‘Near vermilion, one turns red; near ink, one turns black.’ Since that monster lives here, he certainly knows the water. Let us capture him now without killing him, and make him convey Master across the river. Then we can decide what else to do with him.” Bajie said, “Brother, there is no need to hesitate. You go first and capture him, while old Pig stays here to guard Master.” The Pilgrim laughed. “Worthy brother, I dare not boast about that. Old Monkey is not especially skilled at affairs beneath the water. If I merely wish to travel through it, I must form a hand seal and recite the Water-Avoiding Spell before I can move; otherwise I must transform myself into some fish, shrimp, crab, turtle, or the like before I can enter. When it comes to matching skills, whether high in the mountains or among the clouds, whatever strange or ingenious feat may be required, old Monkey can perform it; but business underwater is rather awkward for me.” Bajie said, “In former days old Pig commanded the River of Heaven and had eighty thousand naval troops under my charge, so I did learn something of the ways of water. I only fear he may have a whole clan down there—young and old, seven nests and eight generations of them—and if they all come at once, I may not be able to handle them. Might they not seize me instead?” The Pilgrim said, “When you fight him in the water, do not become absorbed in the battle. You are permitted to lose, not to win. Lure him out, and old Monkey will be waiting to help you strike.” Bajie said, “That is sound advice. I am off.” No sooner had he said he was going than he stripped off his blue brocade robe and shoes. Brandishing his rake in both hands, he parted the waters and employed his skills of former days, leaping through the waves and overturning the billows. He plunged in, descended directly to the riverbed, and strode forward.

p.src: Now the Great Sage stood beside Tang Sanzang, protecting him and watching anxiously as the other two fought upon the water, for he himself could not readily join the fray. Then Bajie made a feint with his rake, pretended defeat, turned, and fled toward the eastern bank. The monster pursued close behind and was nearly at the bank. Unable to restrain himself any longer, the Pilgrim left his master, whipped out his iron staff, leapt to the riverbank, and struck straight at the monster's head. The creature dared not meet the blow and, with a swish, plunged back into the river. Bajie shouted, “You Bimawen—you truly are an impatient monkey! If only you had waited a little longer and let me lure him onto higher ground, then blocked the riverbank so he could not turn back, would we not have caught him? Now that he has gone back in, who knows when he will consent to come out again?” The Pilgrim laughed. “Idiot, stop shouting, stop shouting. Let us go back and see Master for now.”

p.src: Bajie went with the Pilgrim up the high bank, where they rejoined Sanzang. Sanzang rose slightly and said, “You have worked hard, disciples.” Bajie said, “Never mind our exertions. Only when we have subdued the monster and carried you across the river will our plan be fully secure.” Sanzang asked, “How did your battle with the monster go just now?” Bajie replied, “That monster's skill makes him a match for old Pig. In the midst of the fight I feigned defeat, and he pursued me right up to the bank. But when he saw Elder Brother raise his staff, he fled.” Sanzang said, “Then what are we to do?” The Pilgrim replied, “Do not worry, Master, and do not distress yourself. It is late now, so sit here upon the cliff while old Sun goes to beg some vegetarian food. Eat and sleep, and tomorrow we shall decide what to do.” Bajie said, “That makes sense. Go quickly and return quickly.”

p.src: The Pilgrim hastily sprang onto a cloud and flew away. Due north he found a household, begged a bowlful of vegetarian food, and returned to offer it to his master. Seeing how swiftly he had returned, Master said, “Wukong, why not go to the household where you begged the food and ask them how we might cross the river? Would that not be better than contending with this monster?” The Pilgrim laughed. “That household is exceedingly far away—some five to seven thousand li from here. How could they know the nature of this river? What good would it do to ask them?” Bajie said, “Elder Brother, there you go lying again. If it is five to seven thousand li away, how did you make the round trip so quickly?” The Pilgrim replied, “What do you know of it? With one somersault, old Sun's cloud carries him one hundred and eight thousand li. For a trifling five or seven thousand li, I need only nod my head twice and bend my waist once to go there and back. What difficulty is there in that?” Bajie said, “Brother, if it is so easy, carry Master on your back, nod your head a couple of times, bend your waist, and leap across. Why go to such pains fighting this monster?” The Pilgrim said, “Can you not ride the clouds? Why do you not carry Master across?” Bajie replied, “Master's mortal flesh and bones are heavier than Mount Tai. How could one such as I, who merely rides the clouds, lift him? Only your somersault cloud could do it.” The Pilgrim said, “My somersault, after all, is merely another way of riding the clouds; it only carries me somewhat farther. If you cannot carry him, how could I? As the ancient saying goes: ‘To move Mount Tai is as easy as lifting a mustard seed; to carry a mortal beyond the red dust is hard.’ When vicious fiends and venomous monsters use carrying spells or conjure winds, they merely drag their victims along the ground; they cannot bear them away through the air. Old Sun knows how to perform tricks of that sort as well. I also know every one of such arts as invisibility and shrinking the earth. But Master must traverse foreign lands to their furthest reaches and cannot be lifted bodily from the sea of suffering; that is why every single step is hard. You and I can only serve as his protectors, preserving his body and his life. We cannot suffer these hardships in his stead, nor can we obtain the scriptures for him; even if we could go ahead and meet the Buddha first, the Buddha would not willingly give the scriptures to you or me. It is just as the saying goes: ‘What is easily gained is lightly valued.’” Hearing this, the idiot murmured his assent and accepted the lesson. They then ate some plain vegetarian food without side dishes, and master and disciples rested beneath the eastern cliff beside the River of Flowing Sands.

The Pilgrim said, “Let us go and see Master for now.”

p.src: The two returned to the high bank and, upon seeing the Tang Monk, told him in full how difficult the monster was to capture. His eyes brimming with tears, the elder said, “With such difficulties before us, how are we ever to cross?” The Pilgrim said, “Master, do not distress yourself. That monster is lurking deep beneath the water, which makes matters truly difficult. Bajie, stay here and protect Master. Do not fight him again while I make a journey to the Southern Sea and back.” Bajie asked, “Brother, what business have you in the Southern Sea?” The Pilgrim replied, “This enterprise of fetching the scriptures was ordained by the Bodhisattva Guanyin; and it was also the Bodhisattva Guanyin who delivered and released us. Now that the River of Flowing Sand blocks our road and we cannot advance, how can the matter be resolved without her? I shall go and ask for her aid; that will be far better than fighting this fiend.” Bajie said, “Quite right, quite right. Brother, when you go, be sure to convey my respects and say that I remain deeply grateful for her former guidance.” Tripitaka said, “Wukong, if you mean to seek the Bodhisattva’s help, do not delay. Go quickly and return quickly.”

p.src: The Pilgrim immediately mounted his somersault cloud and headed straight for the Southern Sea. Ah! In less than half an hour, Mount Putuo was already in sight. Presently he dropped from his somersault outside the Purple Bamboo Grove, where the deities of the twenty-four divisions came forward to greet him, asking, “What brings the Great Sage here?” The Pilgrim said, “My master is in peril, so I have come especially to pay my respects to the Bodhisattva.” The deities said, “Please be seated while we report your arrival.” The deities on duty went directly to the entrance of the Cave of Tidal Sound and reported, “Sun Wukong seeks an audience on urgent business.” The Bodhisattva was beside the Precious Lotus Pool with the Dragon Girl Who Holds the Pearl, leaning on the railing and admiring the flowers. Upon hearing the report, she returned behind the cloudy crags, opened the gate, and summoned him inside. The Great Sage composed himself solemnly, took refuge, and bowed in homage.

p.src: The Bodhisattva asked, “Why are you not protecting the Tang Monk? What has brought you to see me again?” The Pilgrim reported, “Bodhisattva, at Gao Village my master took another disciple named Zhu Bajie, to whom you graciously gave the religious name Wuneng. We have only just passed Yellow Wind Ridge and have now reached the eight-hundred-li River of Flowing Sand, whose three thousand leagues of Weak Water are already impossible for my master to cross. There is also a monster in the river, highly skilled in combat. Wuneng has labored greatly, fighting him three times upon the water, but he could not prevail. The monster blocks our way, and we cannot cross. For this reason I have come especially to inform you, Bodhisattva, and beg you in compassion to help him cross.” The Bodhisattva said, “You monkey are being smug again. Were you unwilling to tell him that you protect the Tang Monk?” The Pilgrim replied, “We only wanted to capture him and make him carry my master across the river. As for affairs beneath the water, I have no great mastery of them. Wuneng found his lair and spoke with him, but I suppose he never mentioned our mission to fetch the scriptures.” The Bodhisattva said, “That monster in the River of Flowing Sand is the Curtain-Raising General descended to the mortal world. He too is a faithful convert whom I exhorted and instructed to protect the scripture pilgrim. Had you said that you were the scripture pilgrims from the Eastern Land, he would never have contended with you and would certainly have submitted.” The Pilgrim said, “The monster now fears battle and refuses to come ashore. He keeps himself hidden in the water, so how can we make him submit? And how is my master to cross the Weak Water?” The Bodhisattva at once summoned Huian, took a little red gourd from her sleeve, and instructed him, “Take this gourd and go with Sun Wukong to the surface of the River of Flowing Sand. Simply call ‘Wujing,’ and he will emerge. First induce him to take refuge with the Tang Monk. Then string his nine skulls together and arrange them according to the Nine Palaces. Place this gourd in their midst, and they will form a magic boat capable of carrying the Tang Monk across the bounds of the River of Flowing Sand.”

p.src: Hearing this, Huian respectfully obeyed his master’s command. Carrying the gourd, he left the Cave of Tidal Sound with the Great Sage and, bearing the Bodhisattva’s decree, took leave of the Purple Bamboo Grove. A poem bears witness to this.

p.src: Before long, the two lowered their clouds and arrived on the bank of the River of Flowing Sand. Zhu Bajie recognized the Pilgrim Mucha—also written “Nezha”—and led his master forward to welcome him. Mucha—also written “Nezha”—exchanged courtesies with Tripitaka and then greeted Bajie. Bajie said, “Through your former guidance, Venerable One, I was able to meet the Bodhisattva. I, Old Zhu, have indeed obeyed her teaching and am now delighted to have entered the Buddhist order. I have been hurrying along the road ever since and had no chance to offer my thanks. Forgive me, forgive me.” The Pilgrim said, “Let us save our reminiscences for later and go call that fellow out.” Tripitaka asked, “Whom are you going to call?” The Pilgrim replied, “I saw the Bodhisattva and related everything that happened. The Bodhisattva said that the monster in the River of Flowing Sand was the Curtain-Raising General descended to the mortal world. For an offense in Heaven, he fell into this river and, forgetting his true nature, became a monster. The Bodhisattva once converted him, and he vowed to submit to Master and journey to the Western Heaven. But because we never mentioned our mission to fetch the scriptures, we fought so bitterly. The Bodhisattva has now sent Mucha—also written “Nezha”—with this gourd to join it with the fellow’s possessions and form a magic boat that will carry you across.” Hearing this, Tripitaka prostrated himself repeatedly in gratitude. Bowing to Mucha—also written “Nezha”—he said, “Venerable One, I earnestly beg you to act without delay.” Holding the gourd securely, Mucha—also written “Nezha”—rode half on cloud and half on mist straight to the surface of the River of Flowing Sand. In a stern voice he cried, “Wujing! Wujing! The scripture pilgrim has been here a long while. Why have you still not submitted?”

p.src: Now the monster, fearing the Monkey King, had returned to the riverbed and was resting in his lair when he suddenly heard someone call his religious name. He knew at once that this concerned the Bodhisattva Guanyin; and when he also heard the words “the scripture pilgrim is here,” he no longer feared axe or halberd. He hastily churned the waves and thrust his head above the surface, where he recognized the Pilgrim Mucha—also written “Nezha.” See how he came forward all smiles, bowed, and said, “Venerable One, forgive me for failing to welcome you. Where is the Bodhisattva now?” Mucha—also written “Nezha”—replied, “My master has not come. She first sent me to instruct you to lose no time in becoming a disciple of the Tang Monk. She commands that the skulls hanging from your neck be joined with this gourd and arranged according to the Nine Palaces to form a magic boat, so that you may carry him across this Weak Water.” Wujing asked, “Where is the scripture pilgrim?” Mucha—also written “Nezha”—pointed with his hand and said, “Is that not he, seated on the eastern bank?” Wujing saw Bajie and said, “That insolent creature came from goodness knows where and fought me without cease these past two days. When did he ever utter a single word about fetching scriptures?” Then he saw the Pilgrim and said, “And that formidable fellow is his helper. He is far too fierce. I will not go.” Mucha—also written “Nezha”—said, “That one is Zhu Bajie, and this one is Sun the Pilgrim. Both are disciples of the Tang Monk, and both were converted by the Bodhisattva. Why should you fear them? Come with me now to meet the Tang Monk.”

p.src: Only then did Wujing put away his treasured staff, straighten his yellow brocade robe, and leap ashore. Falling to his knees before the Tang Monk, he said, “Master, this disciple was blind and failed to recognize your venerable person. I have offended you greatly; I beg you to forgive me.” Bajie said, “You good-for-nothing, why did you not submit earlier instead of insisting on fighting me? What have you to say for yourself?” Pilgrim laughed and said, “Brother, do not blame him. After all, we had never told him about our quest for the scriptures or given him our names.” The elder said, “Are you truly willing to embrace our faith with a sincere heart?” Wujing replied, “This disciple was once instructed and converted by the Bodhisattva. She gave me Sha as my surname and bestowed on me the religious name Sha Wujing. How could I possibly refuse to follow you, Master?” Sanzang said, “If that is so,” and called out, “Wukong, bring the ordination knife and shave his head.” The Great Sage obeyed, taking the ordination knife and shaving his head. Wujing then bowed again to Sanzang and also to Pilgrim and Bajie, establishing their order of seniority. Seeing that his observance of the rites truly displayed the bearing of a monk, Sanzang also called him Monk Sha. Mucha—also written “Zha”—said, “Now that he has received the precepts, there is no need for further chatter. Hurry and make the Dharma boat.”

p.src: Wujing dared not delay. He immediately removed the skulls hanging from his neck, tied them with a cord into a ninefold arrangement, placed the Bodhisattva’s gourd in the center, and invited his master to come down to the riverbank. The elder then boarded the Dharma boat and sat upon it; indeed, it was as steady as a light skiff. Bajie supported him on the left, while Wujing upheld him on the right; behind them, Sun the Pilgrim led the dragon-horse and followed, half in cloud and half in mist; and directly overhead Mucha—also written “Zha”—guarded them. Thus the master floated safely across the bounds of the River of Flowing Sands, passing over that perilous stream amid calm waves and gentle winds. They truly sped like a flying arrow, and before long he reached the farther shore and escaped the surging waters; without being mired in mud or drenched in water, they were fortunate to keep hands and feet perfectly dry; serene and unencumbered, master and disciples set foot on solid ground. Mucha—also written “Zha”—lowered his auspicious cloud and retrieved the gourd. Then the skulls suddenly dissolved into nine currents of dark wind and silently vanished from sight. Sanzang bowed his thanks to Mucha—also written “Zha”—and made reverent obeisance to the Bodhisattva. Indeed:
